name: Chí Phèo
blurb: Nam Cao's 1941 story of a village outcast who wants to be a decent man again
title: Chí Phèo Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: Nam Cao's Chí Phèo explained: who Chí Phèo, Bá Kiến and Thị Nở are, a full plot summary, what the ending means and the themes teachers ask about.
h1: Chí Phèo: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Chí Phèo is a short story by the Vietnamese writer Nam Cao, written in 1941 and first published that year in a collection called Đôi lứa xứng đôi. It is set in Vũ Đại, a poor village in northern Vietnam under French colonial rule. The title character is a man the whole village fears, a drunk and hired thug, and the story traces how he got that way and whether he can change. It is one of the most studied works of modern Vietnamese literature.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: An abandoned child who grows up in Vũ Đại and becomes a farmhand
The village's most powerful landlord and official, cunning and ruthless
A poor, simple and very plain woman who lives with her aunt by the river
Thị Nở's aunt, the head of their small household
Bá Kiến's son, the village head

body: The story opens in the middle of things: Chí Phèo walks along the village road, drunk, cursing the sky, the whole village of Vũ Đại and whoever gave birth to him. Nobody answers, because nobody wants trouble with him. The narrator then goes back to tell his life.

Origins. One morning a man setting eel traps found a newborn baby wrapped in rags beside an old, abandoned brick kiln. The child passed from a blind widow to a craftsman who made rice mortars, then grew up working for one household after another. Around the age of twenty he was a farmhand for Bá Kiến, then still called Lý Kiến. He was honest and quiet, and he felt only shame when Bá Kiến's young third wife kept calling him in to massage her legs.

Prison. Bá Kiến grew jealous and had Chí sent to prison on a pretext. Seven or eight years later Chí came back a different man: a shaved head, teeth scraped white, tattoos and a hard face that looked like a bandit's. On his first day home he got drunk, took a knife to Bá Kiến's gate, cursed him and slashed his own face to make a scene. Bá Kiến calmed the crowd, spoke to Chí kindly, gave him money and food, and soon used him as a hired thug, sending him to collect debts and deal with men who threatened Bá Kiến's position. Chí drank all the time and lost track of how many lives and homes he had wrecked. The village called him the devil of Vũ Đại.

Thị Nở. One moonlit night, drunk, Chí comes upon Thị Nở asleep under the banana trees by the river near his hut, and they spend the night together. Next morning he wakes up sick and sober for the first time in years. He hears ordinary sounds outside, the market, the boats, and remembers his old dream of a small family with a wife and a little land. Thị Nở comes back with a pot of hot onion rice porridge she has cooked for him. No one has ever cared for him like this; he eats it and cries. He begins to hope that she could help him return to an honest life and among people, and he asks her to come and live with him.

Rejection. Thị Nở goes home to ask her aunt. The aunt is furious that her niece wants to marry a man with no father, a drunk who only knows how to cause trouble, and berates her. Thị Nở returns and repeats every insult to Chí, then leaves him. Chí drinks, but this time the liquor does not make him drunk. He smells the onion porridge again, cries, takes his knife and goes out saying he will kill Thị Nở and her aunt.

Instead of going to Thị Nở's house, Chí walks straight to Bá Kiến's. He accuses Bá Kiến of making him what he is and says he wants to be an honest man again but no one will let him, and that he knows he can never go back, because no one can erase the scars on his face. Then he stabs Bá Kiến to death and cuts his own throat. The villagers come to look at the two bodies and say, almost with relief, that the two devils have killed each other. At home, Thị Nở hears the news, remembers their nights together, looks down at her belly and thinks of the old, deserted brick kiln far away.

The literal events are clear; the meaning comes from what Nam Cao implies. Chí's last words ask who will allow him to be decent, and by killing Bá Kiến he strikes at the power that took his life from him, not at Thị Nở, who only refused him. His death shows that a man pushed outside the community cannot be let back in, even when his human feelings have returned.

Thị Nở's glance at the kiln closes a circle. Chí was found as a baby beside that kiln, and the image suggests she may be pregnant and that another abandoned child, another Chí Phèo, could be born into the same village. Most critics read this as Nam Cao's warning that while the same conditions remain, the tragedy will repeat. The story's first title, Cái lò gạch cũ (The Old Brick Kiln), points to exactly this image.

ul: Dehumanisation: an honest farmhand is turned into a thug by an unjust prison system and by a landlord who uses him, both body and soul.
The wish to be human: Thị Nở's onion porridge shows that Chí's decency was never fully gone, and his desire to be accepted again is the centre of the story.
Exclusion: the village rejects Chí completely, and the aunt's refusal shows that even a small hope cannot cross that wall.
Power and exploitation: Bá Kiến rules Vũ Đại by playing people against each other, using thugs like Chí to protect his position.
Cycles of misery: the opening curse, the brick kiln and the ending suggest that the same conditions will produce the same tragedy again.
Length: a short story that takes about an hour to read; it is a standard text in the Vietnamese upper-secondary literature curriculum.

Titles: Nam Cao called it Cái lò gạch cũ (The Old Brick Kiln); the publisher Đời Mới printed it in 1941 in a collection retitled Đôi lứa xứng đôi (A Perfect Match), and Nam Cao renamed it Chí Phèo when it was reprinted in 1946.
Adaptations: the 1982 film Làng Vũ Đại ngày ấy combines Chí Phèo with Nam Cao's Lão Hạc and Sống mòn; an English translation appeared in Chi Pheo and Other Stories (Hanoi, 1961).
Content: drunkenness, violence, a murder and a suicide, and sex outside marriage, described plainly but without detail.

What teachers usually ask about: Chí's transformation from farmhand to devil of Vũ Đại, the bowl of onion porridge, his final speech before killing Bá Kiến, the brick kiln image, and Nam Cao's humanism and realism.

check.q: Why did Chí Phèo first go to prison?
options: He killed a man in a fight
Bá Kiến was jealous of him and had him jailed
He was caught stealing from the market
check.why: Bá Kiến grew jealous because his third wife kept calling the young farmhand in, and he had Chí sent to prison.

check.q: What makes Chí Phèo want to change his life?
options: Thị Nở's care, shown by a bowl of onion porridge
A sermon from the village monk
Money left to him by Bá Kiến
check.why: When he wakes sick and sober, Thị Nở brings him onion porridge, and her kindness makes him hope to live honestly.

check.q: What does Thị Nở think of at the very end of the story?
check.why: She looks at her belly and thinks of the kiln where Chí was found as a baby, hinting the tragedy could repeat.

faq.q: Why does Chí Phèo kill Bá Kiến and not Thị Nở?
faq.a: He sets out to kill Thị Nở and her aunt, but his anger turns to the man who made him a thug; he blames Bá Kiến for taking away his chance to be an honest man.

faq.q: Is Thị Nở pregnant at the end of Chí Phèo?
faq.a: The story only hints at it: she looks at her belly and thinks of the brick kiln where Chí was abandoned. Nam Cao leaves it unstated.

faq.q: What is the most famous line in Chí Phèo?
faq.a: Chí's cry to Bá Kiến that he wants to be an honest man but no one will let him, which sums up the whole story.
